subject: Computing
source: National Curriculum KS2 Computing (computer networks and the internet, search technologies, selection in programs); unplugged packets activity and Scratch work adapted from the school's Drive Computing scheme (Compute-IT 'How the web works' / ComputerScienceUK) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9, v3): Tarbiyyah Primary computing long-term plan 2023-24 Year 4 Spring 1 (Repetition in Shapes; Data Logging), NCCE Teach Computing based

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Networks, the internet and searching
lessons.title: How the internet works
objectives: Explain what a network and the internet are
Describe how a message is split into packets and sent
Tell the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web

keywords.def: computers and devices joined together to share information
a huge network of networks across the world
a small piece of a message sent across a network
a device that sends data to the right place

starter: Bismillah. Name three devices that can connect to Wi-Fi.
What is an input device? Give an example.
How do you think a photo gets from your phone to a friend's phone?

teach.heading: What is a network?
bullets: Devices joined so they can share information.
A home network: phones, tablets, router.
School networks share printers and files.
teach.note: Draw your own home network on screen: router in the middle with lines to devices. Ask pupils how many devices are connected in their homes. Explain that the router is the device that connects them to the internet.

teach.heading: The internet
bullets: The internet is a network of networks.
Cables under the sea and wires join countries.
Servers are computers that store websites.
teach.note: Show a world map with cable routes (many internet connections between continents travel through undersea cables). Say clearly that the internet is not 'the cloud in the sky'; it is real cables, routers and servers. Misconception: pupils say 'the internet is Wi-Fi'; Wi-Fi is only the last wireless step to the router.

teach.heading: Packets
bullets: Big messages are split into small packets.
They are put back in order at the end.
teach.note: Do the unplugged activity: write the sentence 'Bismillah, I am learning about packets' with one word on each card. Number the cards. Shuffle and send 'by different routes' (pupils pass them around), then rebuild in order. Link this to why numbering is important.

teach.heading: Internet or web?
bullets: The World Wide Web is websites on it.
Email and games use the internet but are not websites.
teach.note: Use the analogy of roads and shops: the internet is the road system, the web is the shops on the roads. Ask: is a video call the web? (It uses the internet; it is not necessarily a web page.) Accept discussion; the key idea is that the web runs on the internet.

practice: Which is bigger, a network or the internet? Explain in one sentence.
Why are packets numbered? (so they can be put back in the right order)
True or false: all packets must take the same route.
independent: Draw your home network with at least 4 devices and a router, and label each part.
Split the sentence 'Please send the file to my friend' into 6 packets, number them, shuffle and swap with a partner to rebuild.
Write three sentences explaining the difference between the internet and the web.
exit: What is the job of a router?
lessons.homework: Count how many devices in your home connect to the internet and list them with the type of each (phone, TV, console, etc.).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled diagrams and a word bank; allow pupils to rebuild the packet sentence physically. Stretch: ask what happens if one packet goes missing.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Networks, the internet and searching
lessons.title: Searching the web and checking if it is trustworthy
objectives: Use keywords to search effectively
Spot adverts and sponsored results
Check whether a website can be trusted

keywords.def: a website which finds web pages for the words you type
an important word used in a search
something you can trust to be true

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between the internet and the web?
Where would you look to find out how tall Mount Everest is?

teach.heading: Choosing keywords
bullets: 'Tallest mountain world' beats a long sentence.
Add words to narrow the search.
teach.note: Search live for 'mountain' and then 'tallest mountain in the world height metres'. Compare the results. Ask pupils to say which keywords gave a better answer. Use a child-safe search engine or safe search if available.

teach.heading: Adverts and results
bullets: Adverts want you to buy or click.
teach.note: Point to the labels on a real results page. Ask: who pays for an advert, and what do they want you to do? Remind pupils never to click on pop-ups or download things without asking a trusted adult.

teach.heading: Can I trust this page?
bullets: Do other sites say the same thing?
Is it trying to sell something?
teach.note: Compare two pages on the same topic: one from a museum or a school, one a personal blog with adverts. Ask pupils to apply the four checks. Teach that if something is shared online but not checked, we should be careful, and that checking before repeating information is part of honesty (sidq).

teach.heading: Fact or opinion
bullets: Fact: Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level.
Opinion: Everest is the best mountain.
teach.note: Give pupils five statements to sort into fact or opinion. Misconception: pupils think if it is on the internet it is true. Show a made-up news story (clearly labelled as fake for the lesson) and ask how they could check it.

practice: Which keywords would you use to find the date of Eid al-Fitr this year? Choose from: when, Eid al-Fitr, date, 2026, please tell me.
Is this a fact or an opinion? 'The Thames is a river in London.' 'Football is the best sport.'
Name two ways to check if a website is trustworthy.
independent: Use a search engine to find out the length of the River Nile. Write the answer and the website you used.
Find two websites with the answer. Do they agree? Which seems more reliable and why?
Make a poster with 'Four questions to ask about a website'.
exit: Write two good keywords to find out about volcanoes.
Name one reason why a website might not be reliable.
lessons.homework: Find a fact about your favourite animal from two different websites. Write both sources down and say if they agree.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a checklist with icons and sentence starters ('I trust this website because...'). Stretch: investigate how a page's address (URL) can help show who made it.

lessons.title: Selection: if, then, else
objectives: Explain that selection lets a program make a choice
Write simple if-then-else rules using a condition
Predict the output of a selection algorithm

keywords.def: choosing which instructions to follow
a question with a yes or no answer
the word we use to check a condition

starter: Bismillah. How many sides does a square have?
If it is raining, what do you take with you? What if it is not raining?

teach.heading: Everyday choices
bullets: If it is raining, take an umbrella.
A condition is a yes or no question.
teach.note: Ask pupils to stand if the condition is true. Use: 'If you are wearing a blue top, stand up'. The condition is 'wearing a blue top?' and the answer is yes or no. Link to making choices carefully.

teach.heading: If, then, else
bullets: IF it is Friday THEN go to Jumu'ah.
ELSE go to school as normal.
teach.note: Display the flow as a diamond decision shape with two arrows. Ask pupils which path they follow on Mondays. Only one path is followed; misconception: pupils think the program does both.

teach.heading: Number conditions
teach.note: Explain the symbols: greater than (>), less than (<), equal to (=). Test with different scores: 5, 10, 11. Many pupils get 10 wrong: 10 is not greater than 10, so the else branch runs.

teach.heading: Unplugged robot rule
bullets: IF the robot is next to a wall THEN turn right.
Follow the rule on a grid.
teach.note: Use a drawn grid with walls around the edges and a counter. Pupils follow the rule step by step. Ask for predictions then check. This builds the idea of a program which responds to its situation.

practice: IF age is 8 or more THEN 'You can join the club' ELSE 'Come back next year'. What is said for age 7? For age 9?
Complete: IF the light is red THEN ___ ELSE ___.
IF score > 10 THEN 'Well done' ELSE 'Try again'. What is said for 10?
independent: Write three if-then-else rules for a robot that chooses what to wear based on the weather.
Draw a flowchart with a decision diamond for 'Is it Friday?'.
Create a quiz question with an if-then-else response for a right and wrong answer.
exit: IF number > 5 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small'. What is said for 3?
lessons.homework: Write three if-then-else rules that describe decisions you make in a normal day.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use colour-coded cards (green IF, orange THEN, blue ELSE) and physical movement for the paths. Stretch: write a rule with two conditions joined with AND.

lessons.title: Selection in Scratch: a quiz
objectives: Use if-then-else blocks in Scratch
Use ask and answer to take input from the user
Build and debug a short quiz

keywords.def: a block that asks a question and waits for typed input
the block which stores what the user typed
a block that chooses between two sets of instructions

starter: Bismillah. What does a condition give: yes/no or a number?
IF 7 > 5 THEN 'yes' ELSE 'no'. What is said?

teach.heading: Ask and answer
teach.note: Build live: when green flag clicked, ask 'What is the capital of France?' and wait. Show the answer block holding the reply by making the sprite say it. Explain that this is input from the user.

teach.heading: If-else block
bullets: Put the condition in the diamond.
teach.note: Build the if-else around the answer check. Stress that the equals block compares the answer with the text. Mention that Scratch ignores upper or lower case for text, so 'paris' also matches. Misconception: forgetting to put the if-else block after the ask block.

teach.heading: Test every path
teach.note: Run the quiz twice, once right and once wrong. Discuss why testing both paths matters: a bug can hide in the path we did not try. Praise pupils who test carefully.

teach.heading: More questions
teach.note: Show how to copy and edit the blocks for another question. If time, show how a variable can count correct answers, but do not require it yet. Questions can be about Islamic knowledge such as the number of daily prayers (5).

practice: Which block gives the text the user typed?
What is wrong? The if-else block is placed before the ask block. (the program checks before the user answers)
Predict: the answer is '5'. IF answer = 5 THEN say 'Correct'. What happens?
independent: Build a 3-question quiz in Scratch with if-else feedback for each answer.
Test every question with a right and a wrong answer and write down any bug you fix.
Swap quizzes with a partner and give one improvement.
exit: Which Scratch block takes input from the user?
Why do we test both the right and wrong answer?
lessons.homework: Add two more questions to your quiz, about a subject you love, and test it with someone at home.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a partially built quiz with the blocks in order to complete. Stretch: add a variable called score and add 1 for each correct answer.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Repetition in shapes and data logging
lessons.title: What is a loop? Repeating instructions unplugged
lessons.bigQuestion: How could you tell a friend to walk around the edge of a square table using only one sentence?
objectives: To understand that a loop repeats a set of instructions a chosen number of times
successCriteria: All: find the repeating part of a set of instructions
Most: rewrite instructions using 'repeat ... times'
Some: work out how many times to repeat to draw a shape
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: properties of shapes and right angles

keywords.def: do the same instructions again
instructions that run again and again
one step that tells someone what to do
instructions in order

hook.text: How could you tell a friend to walk around the edge of a square table using only one sentence?
hook.a: 'Repeat 4 times: walk one side, turn right.' That one sentence is a loop.

starter.q: An algorithm is... A) a set of steps in order B) a type of computer C) a website
starter.a: A) a set of steps in order
options: A set of steps in order

starter.a: A mistake in a program or algorithm.

starter.q: How many sides does a square have?
How many degrees is a right-angle turn?

teach.heading: Patterns in instructions
bullets: Some steps come again and again
teach.note: Read out: 'forward 3, turn right, forward 3, turn right, forward 3, turn right, forward 3, turn right'. Ask: what do you notice?

teach.heading: A loop
teach.note: The repeating part goes inside the loop.

teach.heading: Draw a square on paper
teach.note: Pupils follow the loop with a pencil on a dot grid (pupil PDF).

model.problem: Draw a square with sides of 3 dots.
steps: Start at a dot, pencil facing up

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which part of 'jump, clap, jump, clap, jump, clap' goes inside the loop?
check.why: The pair 'jump, clap' repeats 3 times: repeat 3 (jump, clap).

practice.q: Write as a loop: 'step, step, step, step, step'.
practice.model: Teacher counts the repeats aloud: '1, 2, 3, 4, 5 steps', so repeat 5 with 'step' inside.

practice.q: Write as a loop: 'forward 2, turn right' four times.
What shape does 'repeat 4 (forward 5, turn right 90)' draw?

independent.q: Core: On the dot grid, follow 'repeat 4 (forward 4, turn right 90)' and draw the shape.
independent.a: A square with sides of 4 dots.
independent.model: Teacher draws the first side and turn on the shared grid.

independent.q: Extend: Write a loop that draws a rectangle 4 long and 2 wide. Hint: put two sides inside the loop.
independent.a: repeat 2 (forward 4, turn right 90, forward 2, turn right 90)

independent.q: Stretch: Write a loop for a 'staircase' of 3 steps (up 1, right 1).
independent.a: repeat 3 (forward 1, turn right 90, forward 1, turn left 90)

exit.q: A loop... A) repeats instructions B) deletes instructions C) stops a program
Write a loop for walking around a square table.

lessons.homework: Find a loop in daily life (for example the steps of wudu repeated three times) and write it as 'repeat __ times: ...'.
lessons.send: SEND: arrows to cut out and stick. EAL: repeat, forward, turn with gestures. Stretch: write a loop inside a loop.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Repetition in shapes and data logging
lessons.title: Drawing shapes with the repeat block
lessons.bigQuestion: To walk all the way around any shape and face the way you started, how far must you turn in total?
objectives: To understand how a repeat block and the pen draw regular shapes on screen
successCriteria: All: draw a square with a repeat block
Most: draw a triangle and a hexagon by changing the count and angle
Some: explain the rule: turn = 360 divided by the number of sides
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: angles in regular shapes (turns adding to 360 degrees)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the hexagons of the honeycomb, made by bees as Allah inspired them (an-Nahl 16:68)

keywords.def: a block that runs the blocks inside it again
how far the sprite turns, in degrees
the extension that lets a sprite draw
a closed figure like a square or triangle

hook.text: To walk all the way around any shape and face the way you started, how far must you turn in total?

starter.q: Write a loop for a square.
How many degrees in a full turn? A) 90 B) 180 C) 360

starter.a: Writing the same instructions again (time and mistakes).

starter.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?

teach.heading: Pen and repeat
bullets: pen down to draw, pen up to stop
teach.note: Share screen: use an object sprite (Pencil) and delete the cat. 'erase all' clears the stage.

teach.heading: The square
teach.note: Model live and run.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
erase all
pen down
repeat 4
  move 100 steps
  turn right 90 degrees
end
code.output: A square with sides of 100 steps.

teach.heading: The turn rule
teach.note: Fill the table with the class.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: 3 sides and 360 / 3 = 120 degrees. Turning 60 is the inside angle, a common trap.

practice.q: Build the square script and run it.
practice.model: Teacher builds it block by block, predicting 'a square' before the green flag.

practice.q: Change it to draw a triangle.
What turn do you need for a pentagon (5 sides)?

independent.q: Core: Draw a hexagon with a repeat block.
independent.a: repeat 6 (move 60, turn 60).
independent.model: Teacher works out 360 / 6 = 60 aloud, then builds and runs it.

independent.q: Extend: Draw an octagon (8 sides). Write the turn sum first.
independent.a: 360 / 8 = 45; repeat 8 (move 50, turn 45).

independent.q: Stretch: Try 'repeat 36 (move 10, turn 10)'. What shape appears and why?
independent.a: Almost a circle: 36 x 10 = 360, with many tiny sides.

exit.q: For a square the sprite turns... A) 45 B) 90 C) 120
Explain how to find the turn for any regular shape.
exit.a: Divide 360 by the number of sides.

lessons.homework: Write the loop (repeat count and turn) for a shape with 10 sides. Check: does repeats x turn = 360?
lessons.send: SEND: the table of shapes and turns printed beside the screen. EAL: angle, turn, degrees. Stretch: draw a star with 'repeat 5 (move 100, turn 144)'.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Repetition in shapes and data logging
lessons.title: Patterns: repeating shapes and changing the angle
lessons.bigQuestion: Islamic geometric art turns one simple shape again and again. How many times would you turn a square to make a star pattern?
objectives: To understand how putting a shape loop inside another loop makes a pattern
successCriteria: All: repeat a square to make a pattern
Most: choose the turn between shapes so the pattern goes all the way round
Some: predict a pattern from its script before running it
lessons.smsc: Cultural: geometric pattern in Muslim architecture such as the Alhambra

keywords.def: a design that repeats in a regular way
turn around a point
a loop inside another loop
the number of times a loop repeats

hook.text: Islamic geometric art turns one simple shape again and again. How many times would you turn a square to make a star pattern?

starter.a: 360 divided by the number of sides.

starter.q: Write the loop for a hexagon.
What block stops the pen drawing?

teach.heading: Shapes become patterns
teach.note: Show a geometric tile picture. The same square turned 8 times makes a star.

teach.heading: A loop inside a loop
teach.note: Trace it with your cursor.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
erase all
pen down
repeat 8
  repeat 4
    move 80 steps
    turn right 90 degrees
  end
  turn right 45 degrees
end
code.output: Eight squares turned around one point: an eight-pointed star pattern.

teach.heading: Going all the way round
teach.note: Same rule as last lesson, used for the whole pattern.

model.problem: Make a pattern of 6 triangles all the way round.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A pattern repeats a square 10 times. What turn goes between the squares?
check.why: 360 / 10 = 36. 90 is the turn inside the square, not between squares.

practice.q: Build the 8-square pattern from the slide.
practice.model: Teacher builds the inner square loop first, runs it, then wraps it in 'repeat 8' and adds 'turn 45'.

practice.q: Change it to 12 squares. What turn now?
What happens with 8 squares and turn 30?
practice.a: The pattern does not go all the way round (8 x 30 = 240).

independent.q: Core: Make a pattern of 6 hexagons all the way round.
independent.a: repeat 6 (repeat 6 (move 50, turn 60), turn 60)
independent.model: Teacher writes the two numbers first: inner turn 60 (hexagon), outer turn 360 / 6 = 60.

independent.q: Extend: Add 'change pen colour by 10' in the outer loop. Describe the result.
independent.a: Each shape is a different colour, like a colour wheel.

independent.q: Stretch: Predict, then test, what 'repeat 36 (repeat 4 (move 60, turn 90), turn 10)' draws.
independent.a: 36 squares turned 10 degrees each: a round, flower-like pattern.

exit.q: A loop inside another loop is called... A) a nested loop B) a bug C) a sprite
How do you choose the turn between shapes in a pattern?
exit.a: Divide 360 by the number of shapes.

lessons.homework: Draw on paper one pattern you could make with a nested loop and write its script.
lessons.send: SEND: start from the square loop already built. EAL: rotate, pattern, inside. Stretch: pattern of pentagons (inner turn 72).

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Repetition in shapes and data logging
lessons.title: Debug and improve a shape program
lessons.bigQuestion: Your program drew half a hexagon. Is the mistake more likely in the repeat count or in the turn?
objectives: To understand how to test a shape program, find its bugs and improve it
successCriteria: All: say what a program should draw and what it does draw
Most: find and fix the bug in a shape program
Some: improve a working program so it is shorter or easier to change
lessons.smsc: Moral: patience (sabr) and honesty about our own mistakes

keywords.def: find and fix mistakes
a mistake that makes a program go wrong
run it to check it works
make it better, shorter or clearer

hook.text: Your program drew half a hexagon. Is the mistake more likely in the repeat count or in the turn?

starter.q: Turn between 8 shapes in a full pattern?

starter.a: Clears the drawing from the stage.

teach.heading: Testing
teach.note: A test is only useful if you know what should happen.

teach.heading: Common shape bugs
teach.note: Show four tiny broken scripts, one per bug.

teach.heading: Fix one bug at a time
teach.note: Changing many things at once hides what fixed it.

model.problem: Should draw a hexagon; draws half of one: repeat 3 (move 60, turn 60).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A square program draws a line. Most likely bug?
options: The turn is outside the loop
check.why: If the turn is not inside the loop the sprite never turns between sides.

practice.q: Fix: 'repeat 4 (move 100, turn 60)' should draw a square.
practice.model: Teacher says: expected square, got an open zig-zag; the angle is wrong; 360 / 4 = 90; change and test.

practice.q: Fix: a triangle program draws nothing but the sprite moves.
Fix: the pattern draws on top of the last one every time.

independent.q: Core: Open 'Shape bugs' in the class studio and fix all four programs. Test each one.
independent.a: Square: turn 90; triangle: pen down; hexagon: repeat 6; pattern: turn inside outer loop.
independent.model: Teacher fixes the square live using the three questions.

independent.q: Extend: Improve your hexagon so the size is set in one place (use a 'size' variable or one move block).
independent.a: Use one variable 'size' in move; change it once.

independent.q: Stretch: Write in the portal response box how you found one bug. Start: 'It should have drawn... but it drew... so I...'
independent.a: For example: It should have drawn a hexagon but it drew half, so I changed repeat 3 to repeat 6.

exit.q: After fixing a bug you should... A) delete the program B) test it again C) add more blocks
Why fix one bug at a time?
exit.a: So you know which change fixed it.

lessons.homework: Write a shape program with one bug for a family member to find. Note the fix.
lessons.send: SEND: one bug highlighted at a time. EAL: expected, actual, fix. Stretch: fix a nested-loop pattern with two bugs.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Repetition in shapes and data logging
lessons.title: Data logging: planning a temperature log
lessons.bigQuestion: Is your home the same temperature at breakfast, lunch and bedtime? How could you find out?
objectives: To understand how a data log records measurements at regular intervals
successCriteria: All: say what a data log is
Most: plan when and where to take temperature readings
Some: explain why readings must be taken at equal intervals
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: states of matter and temperature (heating and cooling)

keywords.def: facts or measurements we collect
a record of data taken over time
a device that measures something, like temperature
the time between two readings

hook.text: Is your home the same temperature at breakfast, lunch and bedtime? How could you find out?
hook.a: Measure it at regular times and write it down: a data log.

starter.a: Run the program to check it works.
options: Run it to check it works

starter.q: What is temperature measured in, in science?
Name an instrument that measures temperature.

teach.heading: What is a data log?
teach.note: Weather stations log temperature every hour. Our school day is planned around prayer times that change too.

teach.heading: Sensors
bullets: Data loggers take readings by themselves
teach.note: Show the thermometer and a digital thermometer picture. At home we act as the data logger.

teach.heading: Equal intervals
teach.note: Model the plan table.

teach.heading: Reading the log
bullets: Look for the highest and lowest
A chart shows it at a glance
teach.note: Example values are for practice only.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Every reading is 2 hours apart; the others have different gaps.

practice.q: From the table, when was the kitchen warmest?
practice.model: Teacher runs a finger down the temperature column, finds the biggest number, 21, and reads across: 12:00.

practice.q: How much did it warm up between 8:00 and 12:00?
What is the interval in the table?

independent.q: Core: Plan your own temperature log at home: one room, 5 times, equal intervals. Fill the time and place columns.
independent.model: Teacher fills the first two rows of the plan for the kitchen at 2-hour intervals.

independent.q: Extend: Predict when your room will be warmest and why. Write in the portal response box. Start: 'I predict...'
independent.a: For example: I predict 13:00, because the sun shines in and the heating has been on.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why taking readings 'whenever I remember' would not be fair.
independent.a: The gaps would be different, so we could not compare change over time.

exit.q: A data log records... A) one reading B) readings over time C) a password
What is an interval?

lessons.homework: With a grown-up, use a thermometer (or a weather app) to take your 5 readings and keep the log in your exercise book: it is entered into a spreadsheet in a later lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: the table already drawn with times filled in. EAL: data, reading, interval, sensor. Stretch: log two rooms and compare.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Photo editing and spoken audio editing
lessons.title: Digital images: pixels and photographs
lessons.bigQuestion: If you zoom in very far on a photo, what do you see?
objectives: To understand that digital images are made of pixels and how to take a good photograph of an object
successCriteria: All: explain what a pixel is
Most: compare low and high resolution
Some: take a clear photo of an object using light and framing
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: noticing beauty in Allah's creation through photos of nature

keywords.def: a tiny square of colour that makes up a digital image
how many pixels an image has
a saved piece of work on a computer
what is inside the edges of the photo

hook.text: If you zoom in very far on a photo, what do you see?

teach.heading: Pixels
bullets: Every digital picture is a grid of tiny squares

teach.heading: A good photo
cycle: Choose an object or a plant

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

practice.q: Colour a 6 by 6 pixel grid on the pupil PDF to make a simple shape.
